prize_parts.citation: for foundational contributions to the theory of nominal rigidities, staggered price and wage setting, and monetary policy rules and their microfounded analysis

statement.case_for: I have moved B014 from second to first place. In my opening I put B030 (Grossman-Helpman) first. Reading the other ten openings, no colleague ranks it, and I could not defend ranking it first without a stronger case that protection-for-sale is a distinct advance beyond the 2008 trade prize. On the merits, B014 has the broadest and most durable influence of any shortlisted achievement. Staggered pricing and contracting (Calvo, Taylor) supply the friction on which the microfounded Phillips curve and the policy-analysis apparatus rest. The Taylor rule gave policy a simple, testable and communicable benchmark. Woodford's Interest and Prices turned these pieces into a welfare-based, general-equilibrium theory of optimal monetary policy. Together they changed both the scientific analysis of monetary policy and how central banks think and communicate. I propose Calvo, Taylor and Woodford because each is the clearest originator of a distinct, load-bearing component: the pricing friction, the contract and rule, and the normative synthesis. This is from my own knowledge of the literature and I have not independently verified priority. The framework has decades of confirmation, and critique after 2008 and 2021-22 has led to extensions such as heterogeneous-agent models rather than abandonment.
statement.case_against: Attribution is the strongest reservation. Gali, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Evans, Smets and Wouters have strong claims to the empirical and estimated-DSGE half of the story. A three-person cap forces exclusions that a reader of the field could reasonably call unfair, and the citation therefore leans toward the conceptual foundations rather than the estimation tradition. There is also a real question of marginal contribution after earlier macro prizes (rational expectations, Bernanke in 2022). Finally, the framework's forecasting performance around 2008 and the post-2021 inflation is contested, and some may read this as the prize arriving late for a paradigm that is already being superseded.

responses.point: Tommy ranks B006 (Rubinstein-Wolinsky) first on the strength of a foundational, four-decade-old, unambiguously attributed bargaining result. For B014 he proposes Woodford, Taylor and Gali, with Calvo and Christiano-Eichenbaum as plausible alternatives.
responses.response: I agree that B006 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and I ranked it fourth on that basis. What holds me back from putting it above B014 is breadth of downstream use and the density of recent game-theory recognition (2005, 2007, 2012, 2020), which I would weigh as a narrowing of marginal contribution, not as a verdict on quality. On the B014 trio, I would keep Calvo over Gali. Calvo's 1983 pricing friction is the building block in effectively every New Keynesian model, including Gali's. Gali's contribution is substantial, but it is largely a development and empirical test of that structure. I accept that this is a judgement call, and that his case becomes stronger if the committee prefers a citation weighted toward the empirical framework.

responses.point: Per ranks B003 first. He argues that collateral constraints and credit-cycle amplification are a foundational macro-finance mechanism, and he includes Gertler for the financial accelerator and intermediary work. He acknowledges that the 2022 prize complicates the Bernanke link.
responses.response: I take B003 seriously and ranked it third, and I regard Kiyotaki-Moore as one of the cleanest two-author attributions on the list. I would not add Gertler. His accelerator work with Bernanke sits next to the 2022 recognition of banks and crises, and he also appears in B014. Naming him here would blur the attribution across two entries rather than sharpen it. The question I would put to you is why the mechanism deserves priority over B014 now. The 2022 prize already covered much of the financial-crisis territory, and I am not convinced the marginal gain from recognising collateral-constraint dynamics outweighs recognising the monetary-policy framework. I would not object strongly to B003 as the prize, and it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Timo ranks B047 (Melitz-Helpman) first. He argues that the heterogeneous-firm model moved the unit of analysis in trade from industries to firms and has more than two decades of confirmation. He notes the Krugman 2008 overlap and the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum priority question.
responses.response: I agree that Melitz (2003) is a strong core contribution, and trade has not been recognised since 2008. I have two reservations. First, the priority questions he raises (Bernard-Jensen, Eaton-Kortum, Hopenhayn) involve people who are not credited on this entry, which makes the citation harder to write than B014's. Second, Helpman appears in both B047 and B030. I originally put B030 first, so I should say plainly that it would be inconsistent for me to argue for Helpman in one entry while discounting him in the other. If the committee wants trade, it should decide which Helpman contribution it is rewarding. Right now I think B047 is the stronger of the two trade candidates. That is why B030 is only a low-ranked alternative for me.

responses.point: Anna ranks B014 first with Woodford, Taylor and Calvo. She notes that the field is crowded, that the 2022 prize and earlier monetary-macro awards may have covered this area, and that the post-2021 inflation and the heterogeneous-agent critique may temper enthusiasm.
responses.response: I agree with her trio and with her description of the risks. On the overlap concern, I would distinguish the earlier awards: Lucas, Sargent and Sims addressed expectations and identification, Kydland and Prescott addressed time consistency and rules, and Bernanke's prize concerned banks and crises. None recognised the pricing-friction and policy-rule framework that central banks use directly. On post-2021 inflation, I read the evidence as showing a framework being extended, not discarded, but I would welcome an argument from members who read it the other way.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers Gali to Calvo, or a citation weighted toward estimated DSGE models, given that eight or more strong contributors are credited on B014.
Whether the 2022 prize and earlier macro prizes leave enough marginal room, and whether post-2021 inflation performance and heterogeneous-agent critiques should lower or raise the case.
Whether a two-part configuration such as B014 with B003 is feasible given the three-person cap. My preferred configuration has only one part, so B003 is an alternative, not an addition.
My attribution judgements rest on my background knowledge of the literature and were not independently verified from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the credited B014 candidates (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is apparent from my profile. I disclose co-authorship with committee colleagues Per Krusell (secretary, who ranks B014 first and proposes the same trio), Timo Boppart and Richard Friberg, and IIES colleagueship with Krusell and Boppart. Those ties bear on how I read their arguments, and I have tried not to treat agreement with Krusell as evidence of merit. I have no apparent connection to the B003 or B030 candidates either.
